title: 1 Samuel 24:16–22
context: Saul weeps, calls David more righteous than himself, and acknowledges that David will surely be king. He asks David to swear not to cut off his descendants, and David swears. Yet the two part ways, Saul to his home and David to the stronghold, with no lasting reconciliation.

verses.text: It came to pass, when David had finished speaking these words to Saul, that Saul said, “Is that your voice, my son David?” Saul lifted up his voice and wept.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul asks, Is that your voice, my son David? and weeps aloud. Arminian readers see genuine emotion and a real moment when Saul could have turned from his course, an opportunity he was responsible to take.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Saul’s tears are sincere in the moment, yet later chapters show no lasting change (26:2). They often distinguish emotional remorse from the repentance God works in the heart.

verses.text: He said to David, “You are more righteous than I; for you have done good to me, whereas I have done evil to you.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul says David is more righteous than he, since David has done good and Saul evil. Arminian readers note that the confession echoes Judah’s admission about Tamar (Genesis 38:26), a rare moment of honesty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Saul acknowledging the truth about himself while not turning from his course. Knowledge of one’s sin, without a changed heart, does not by itself produce new obedience.

verses.text: You have declared today how you have dealt well with me, because when the LORD had delivered me up into your hand, you didn’t kill me.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul recognizes that David spared him when the LORD had delivered him into David’s hand. Arminian readers note that Saul now uses the same language David used, seeing the event for what it was.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Saul confesses God’s hand in the event. Providence has exposed the truth to Saul, yet clear sight of God’s work is not the same as submission to it.

verses.text: For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away unharmed? Therefore may the LORD reward you good for that which you have done to me today.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul asks who finds his enemy and lets him go unharmed, and he prays that the LORD will reward David. Arminian readers see Saul recognizing how unusual David’s mercy was, mercy that went beyond what custom expected.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul, unable to repay David himself, asks God to reward him. They see a recognition that good done in faith is finally rewarded by God, not by those who receive it.

verses.text: Now, behold, I know that you will surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hand.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul admits that David will surely be king and that the kingdom will be established in his hand. Arminian interpreters stress that Saul admits this openly yet does not yield in practice, which shows how a person can know God’s will and still resist it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s purpose confessed by the very man who opposes it, echoing Jonathan’s words in 23:17. The kingdom’s future is settled by God’s choice, even as Saul still clings to power.

verses.text: Swear now therefore to me by the LORD that you will not cut off my offspring after me, and that you will not destroy my name out of my father’s house.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul asks David to swear by the LORD not to cut off his descendants or destroy his name. Arminian readers see a father’s concern for his family, and a plea that rests on the mercy David has just shown.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David later shows kindness to Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9; 21:7). They also acknowledge that 2 Samuel 21 records a darker episode involving Saul’s descendants, which readers wrestle with.

verses.text: David swore to Saul. Saul went home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.
verses.arminianNotes: David swears, and the two separate: Saul goes home, and David goes up to the stronghold. Arminian readers note that David keeps his word but wisely does not trust Saul’s change of heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see no real reconciliation. David returns to the stronghold rather than to Saul’s court, recognizing that tears and oaths have not altered Saul’s settled hostility, as chapter 26 confirms.
